In summary, our research is concerned with

the following aspects of astronomical grains: (i) frequency and size distribution of extinction spectra of graphite and silicate classical grains; (ii) frequency and size of extinction spectra of PAHs; and (iii) the relative contribution of the PAHa and classical grains to extinction.
the development of analytic formulas for frequency dependence of absorption and extinction spectra of the interstellar dust components, which are in the use in the astronomical dust models.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
in the wavelength range 2000–4000 Å, the PAHs contribute more than 50% to the extinction by carbonaceous grains and the contribution is more in case of graphite grains.
the PAHs contribute significantly to extinction in the wavelength region 3–20 μm, but their contribution is negligible in the wavelength range 100–1000 μm.

PAHs are the dominant contributor to the extinction in the wavelength range 2–15 μm and that the contribution from the PAHs is comparable to that from the classical grains in the wavelength range from 1.5 to 2 μm.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have presented the analytic formulas for the extinction spectrum for three important interstellar dust constituents, viz., silicate, graphite and PAHs in the wavelength range 100–22,500 Å.

the frequency dependence of extinction efficiency is very much the same for the three components (silicates, graphite and PAHs) of interstellar dust and that the size dependence is also the same for all three types of grains.
the present work and the two previous papers of the series provide a complete and consistent description of the extinction spectra in interstellar dust models.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in order to obtain accurate results for the extinction, scattering and absorption spectra of interstellar grains, one should take into account their size and frequency distribution dependence in a consistent fashion.
the PAHs can contribute to the extinction at shorter wavelengths, i.e., 1000–2000 Å where classical carbonaceous grains are not expected to be present.
PAHs are important in the UV region of the spectrum and their relative contribution to the total extinction increases with decreasing wavelength.
